extracted.intended_audience: patent attorneys, inventors, and legal historians studying early U.S. patent statutes and remedies
extracted.subtask_description: Extract and summarize the substantive legal requirements, procedural rules, and remedial standards set out in early United States patent statutes (Acts of 1790, 1793, 1794, 1800, 1819, 1832, etc.). Useful for understanding historical patentability, specification, challenge, assignment, infringement remedies, and special procedures for aliens and renewals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patent grant authority and basic term (1790, 1793)
rubrics_metrics.description: Letters-patent to be made out in the name of the United States by the Secretary of State (with Secretary at War and Attorney-General), bearing teste by the President, and granting "the sole and exclusive right and liberty" of making, constructing, using, and vending the invention for "any term not exceeding fourteen years."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Two of the named officers may act (1790); in 1793 the Secretary of State may cause letters-patent to be made and they are to be delivered to the Attorney-General for examination and certification within fifteen days. Patents must be recorded in a public book and delivered to the patentee.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specification and models — enablement and distinctness
rubrics_metrics.description: The grantee shall deliver a specification in writing, accompanied with drafts or models and explanations (if the nature admits) "so particular, and said models so exact, as not only to distinguish the invention or discovery from other things before known and used, but also to enable a workman or other person skilled in the art" to make, construct, or use the same.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specification must be filed and certified copies are competent evidence in courts. Requirement appears in 1790 and is restated and expanded in 1793: descriptions must be "full, clear, and exact" and drawings or specimens must be provided where appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public access to specifications and models
rubrics_metrics.description: Upon application to the Secretary of State for a copy of any specification and permission to have similar model(s) made, it is the duty of the Secretary to give such a copy and permit the model(s) to be taken or made at the expense of the applicant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This creates a right of third parties to obtain specification copies and construct models (at their expense) once the specification is filed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Infringement remedy — damages and forfeiture (1790)
rubrics_metrics.description: Any person offending by making, using, employing, or vending a patented thing without consent shall "forfeit and pay" such damages as shall be assessed by a jury, and shall "forfeit to the person aggrieved, the thing or things so devised, made, constructed, used, employed, or vended..." which may be recovered in an action on the case founded on the Act.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The statute contemplates jury-assessed damages plus recovery/forfeiture of infringing items; actions brought as common-law actions on the case.

rubrics_metrics.name: Time-limited equitable/patent-repeal challenges (1790 & 1793)
rubrics_metrics.description: If, within a specified period after issuing (1790: within one year; 1793: within three years), an oath or affirmation is made before the district judge alleging the patent was obtained surreptitiously or by false suggestion, the judge may grant a rule to show cause and, if sufficient cause is not shown, order process leading to repeal of the patent and judgment for repeal if the patentee was not the first inventor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The statute provides a special, expedited post-issuance process (with short statutory windows) to challenge patents alleged to have been obtained by fraud or surreptitiously.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prima facie effect of patent and preservation of defendant's rights
rubrics_metrics.description: Patents and specifications shall be prima facie evidence that the patentee was the first and true inventor and that the specification is truly specified; nevertheless the defendant may plead the general issue and give special matter in evidence (with prior written notice) tending to prove defects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although the patent is prima facie evidence of validity, defendants retain the right to introduce evidence (with required notice) that the specification is incomplete, improper, or that the patentee is not the true inventor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Defenses based on specification concealment, over‑claiming, prior use, or prior description
rubrics_metrics.description: The defendant may prove that the specification filed does not contain the whole truth, contains more than is necessary, that concealment or addition was intended to mislead, that the invention was in use, or described in a prior public work, or that the patentee surreptitiously obtained the patent; in such cases judgment shall be for the defendant and the patent declared void.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Statute enumerates multiple substantive invalidity defenses tied to lack of candor, insufficiency, overclaiming, and lack of novelty (prior use/prior publication).

rubrics_metrics.name: Fees and administrative payments
rubrics_metrics.description: Patentee shall, before receiving patent, pay specified fees for receiving and filing the petition, filing specifications (by copy-sheet), making out the patent, affixing the great seal, and indorsing the day of delivery; later acts require payment into the treasury (e.g., $30 before presenting petition in 1793).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The statutes list per-item fees (e.g., 50 cents for receiving petition, 10 cents per 100 words for specification copies, $2 for making out patent, $1 for affixing seal, etc.) and lump-sum payments in later acts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Improvement patents and limits (1793)
rubrics_metrics.description: A person who discovers an improvement in principle of a machine or process and obtains a patent for that improvement shall not be at liberty to make, use, or vend the original discovery, nor shall the first inventor be at liberty to use the improvement; simply changing the form or proportions of any machine or composition shall not be deemed a discovery.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The statute restricts scope and mutual exclusivity between original patents and later improvements and sets a low bar for what does not qualify as a patentable improvement (mere form/proportion changes).

rubrics_metrics.name: Inventor's oath and detailed disclosure requirements (1793)
rubrics_metrics.description: Every inventor must swear or affirm that he believes he is the true inventor and deliver a written description of the invention and manner of using it "in such full, clear, and exact terms" to distinguish it from prior things and to enable a person skilled in the art to make and use it; machines require explanation of the principle and modes of application, with drawings and written references where applicable, or specimens for compositions; descriptions must be signed and attested by two witnesses and a model delivered if Secretary deems necessary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This codifies an early enablement and written-description requirement with witness attestation and potential model submission.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assignment recording and succession of rights
rubrics_metrics.description: Inventor (or executor/administrator) may assign title and interest; an assignee who records the assignment in the Secretary of State's office shall thereafter stand in the place of the original inventor as to rights and responsibilities, and so for assignees of assigns.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recording assignments transfers both rights and obligations, and recorded assignees occupy the inventor's legal position.

rubrics_metrics.name: Enhanced penalties for infringement (treble, 1793 & 1800)
rubrics_metrics.description: Statutes prescribe enhanced monetary penalties for infringement: in 1793 a penalty of at least three times the price for which the patentee has usually sold or licensed the use; in 1800 a forfeiture equal to three times the actual damage sustained by the patentee.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The statutes contemplate punitive/compensatory multipliers recoverable in an action on the case in federal courts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Arbitration for interfering applications
rubrics_metrics.description: When applications interfere, they shall be submitted to three arbitrators—one chosen by each applicant and the third appointed by the Secretary of State; the arbitrators' award in writing (any two may sign) is final as to granting the patent; refusal to choose an arbitrator results in issuance to the opposite party; for more than two applicants the Secretary may appoint arbitrators.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This provides a non-judicial procedure for resolving priority/interference disputes in the patent office context.

rubrics_metrics.name: Extension of patent privileges to resident aliens and oath concerning prior knowledge (1800, 1832)
rubrics_metrics.description: Rights and privileges respecting patents were extended to aliens who have resided two years (1800) or to residents who have declared intent to become citizens (1832), provided they swear that the invention has not, to the best of their knowledge, been known or used either in this or any foreign country; failure to satisfy certain use/citizenship conditions can render the patent void.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aliens must take an oath of novelty; 1832 adds conditions that patents may become void automatically if the alien patentee fails to introduce the invention into public use within one year, fails to continue public use six months after introduction, or fails to become a citizen as required.

rubrics_metrics.name: Devolution of application rights on inventor's death
rubrics_metrics.description: If an inventor dies before a patent is granted, the right of applying for and obtaining the patent devolves on the legal representatives in trust for heirs at law or devisees, with the oath/affirmation adapted to them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provides continuity of patent claim/administration after inventor's death.

rubrics_metrics.name: Federal court jurisdiction and equitable relief (1819)
rubrics_metrics.description: Circuit Courts of the United States shall have original cognizance, in equity and at law, of all actions arising under U.S. laws granting exclusive rights to inventors, and such courts may grant injunctions according to equity principles to prevent violation of authors' or inventors' rights on such terms and conditions as they deem fit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Confirms federal courts' authority to grant injunctive relief in patent disputes and provides appellate route to the Supreme Court.

rubrics_metrics.name: Publication requirement for expired patents (1832)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Secretary of State must annually report to Congress and publish in two Washington newspapers a list of all patents which have expired within the preceding year, with the patentees' names alphabetically arranged.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This statute establishes a public record and transparency mechanism for expired patents.

rubrics_metrics.name: Procedure and standards for petitions to prolong/renew patents (1832)
rubrics_metrics.description: Application to Congress to prolong or renew a patent must be made before its expiration and notified at least once a month for three months in two Washington newspapers and in the state/territory newspaper where the patentee resides; the petition must set forth grounds, be verified by oath, evidence may be taken before a judge or justice of the peace, and must be accompanied by a statement of the ascertained value of the invention and the patentee's receipts and expenditures to show profit or loss.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sets procedural and evidentiary expectations for congressional extension petitions, including public notice and financial disclosures to justify extension.

rubrics_metrics.name: Remedy for inadvertent noncompliance (reissue for mistakes, 1832 §3)
rubrics_metrics.description: If a patent is invalid or inoperative because any of the terms or conditions prescribed in the inventor's specification were not complied with by inadvertence, accident, or mistake and without fraudulent intent, the Secretary of State may, upon surrender of the patent, grant a new patent for the same invention for the residue of the unexpired period, upon compliance with the statutory terms and conditions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provides an administrative reissue mechanism to cure inadvertent formal defects while preserving rights for the remainder of the term; the new patent remains subject to the same objections and defenses as an original patent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effect of prior state grants
rubrics_metrics.description: Where any State previously granted an exclusive right to an invention before adoption of the federal government, the party claiming that right cannot obtain an exclusive right under the federal act unless he relinquishes his state right and shows such relinquishment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prevents double rights and requires relinquishment of prior state exclusivities before obtaining federal patent rights.

rubrics_metrics.name: Voidance for failure to introduce or continue public use by alien patentees (1832, Chap. 203)
rubrics_metrics.description: Patents issued to aliens under the privileges extended by statute shall cease and become absolutely void (without legal process) if the patentee fails for one year from issue to introduce the invention into public use in the U.S., or if the invention fails to remain publicly used for six months after such introduction, or if the patentee fails to become a citizen as required.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Imposes affirmative commercialization/citizenship conditions on alien patentees; noncompliance triggers automatic voidness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Restoration of suits affected by prior repeal (1794)
rubrics_metrics.description: Suits, actions, process and proceedings previously had under the Act of 1790 which were set aside, suspended, or abated by repeal may be restored at the instance of plaintiff or defendant within one year after passage of the 1794 Act, and parties are entitled to proceed as if the repeal had not occurred, subject to bringing the opposing party into court by ordinary process.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Allows procedural revival of litigations disrupted by statutory repeal, subject to re-summoning defendants as necessary.
